lesson.title: Where the Joules Go: Understanding Electrical Energy
lesson.summary: Introduces electrical energy as the work done moving charge through a potential difference, combining the already familiar ideas of charge and voltage into the single relationship W = QV.
lesson.body:
Electric charge and voltage are two ideas you already carry into this section, and electrical energy is where they combine into something you can actually measure in joules. Charge, measured in coulombs, is the quantity that current physically transports through a wire. Voltage is the potential difference between two points, defined as the work required to move one coulomb of charge from one point to the other, which is exactly why the volt is defined as one joule per coulomb. Put those definitions together and you get a direct formula for the work done, or energy transferred, when charge moves through a potential difference: W equals Q times V.

It helps to lean on a mechanical analogy you likely already know from physics. Lifting a mass m through a height h against gravity stores gravitational potential energy equal to mgh. Moving a charge Q through an electric potential difference V is the electrical equivalent: the charge gains, or gives up, electrical potential energy equal to QV. The higher the voltage a charge falls through, the more energy each coulomb delivers, in exactly the same way a rock dropped from a taller cliff releases more energy on impact. Voltage is, in this sense, a measure of energy per unit charge, and multiplying by the amount of charge that actually moves recovers the total energy.

Consider a 12 volt car battery moving 5 coulombs of charge through the starter motor circuit. The energy delivered is W = QV = 5 C times 12 V = 60 joules. That energy does not vanish, it converts into other forms: mostly heat in the motor windings and mechanical work turning the engine over. If the same battery instead moved 20 coulombs through the same 12 volt difference, the energy delivered would scale linearly to 240 joules, because energy transfer in this simple relationship depends on both how much charge moves and how large a potential difference it crosses.

This is also why electrical energy is fundamentally a bookkeeping quantity for conservation of energy applied to circuits. Whatever energy a source like a battery supplies by pushing charge through its terminals must show up somewhere else: as heat dissipated in a resistor, as light emitted from a bulb filament, as mechanical work in a motor, or as chemical energy stored back into a rechargeable cell. None of it disappears. Tracking QV through every device a charge passes on its journey around a circuit is how you verify that energy in equals energy out.

In practice, engineers rarely talk about individual joules because the numbers get unwieldy. Utility bills use the kilowatt hour, where one kilowatt hour equals 3.6 million joules, and battery capacity is often rated in ampere hours rather than joules directly, because multiplying an ampere hour rating by the battery's nominal voltage gives a quick estimate of stored energy. Underneath all of these practical units, though, is the same simple relationship you just learned: energy is charge times voltage.
